name: Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia
info: Tito's one-party federation of six South Slav republics, which broke with Stalin in 1948, built workers' self-management and the Non-Aligned Movement, and dissolved in the Yugoslav Wars after his death.

facts.founder: Josip Broz Tito and the Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia (AVNOJ)
facts.predecessor: The Kingdom of Yugoslavia, occupied by the Axis in 1941; Democratic Federal Yugoslavia, proclaimed by the AVNOJ at Jajce on 29 November 1943
facts.successor: Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro), recognised as five successor states

t: The Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia was proclaimed on 29 November 1945 after an election in which the People's Front took an average of 85% of the vote; it was renamed the Socialist Federal Republic in 1963.

Expelled from the Cominform on 28 June 1948, Yugoslavia steered between the blocs: it refused the Warsaw Pact and NATO alike, co-founded the Non-Aligned Movement and introduced workers' self-management in June 1950.

After Tito's death on 4 May 1980 debt, inflation and nationalism overwhelmed a collective presidency; the League of Communists dissolved in January 1990 and four republics declared independence between June 1991 and April 1992.
dyk: The Cominform chose 28 June 1948 to expel Yugoslavia: the anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo Field in 1389, the assassination of Archduke Ferdinand at Sarajevo in 1914 and the Vidovdan Constitution of 1921.
ev: On 29 November the Constituent Assembly abolishes the monarchy and proclaims the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia, a one-party state of six people's republics.
On 28 June the Cominform expels Yugoslavia for 'nationalist elements' and 'Trotskyism'; Soviet troops mass on the Hungarian border and 16,000 suspected Cominformists go to Goli Otok.
Workers' self-management is introduced: workers' councils manage enterprises and share their profits.
A new constitution renames the state the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; emigration of workers is legalised and Western travel opens.
The third constitution gives the republics and the provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina wide autonomy; Tito is elected President-for-life.
On 4 May Tito dies; a collective presidency rotating among the republics takes his place as the foreign debt mounts.
The League of Communists of Yugoslavia dissolves along federal lines; multi-party elections bring separatist parties to power outside Serbia and Montenegro.
On 27 April the Federal Council adopts the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for Serbia and Montenegro, formally ending the breakup.

sections.foundation:
The Axis invaded the Kingdom of Yugoslavia on 6 April 1941 and had occupied and carved it up by 17 April. Two resistances arose: the royalist Yugoslav Army in the Homeland and the Communist Partisans under Josip Broz Tito, a pan-Yugoslav movement preaching the 'brotherhood and unity' of the Yugoslav nations. Its political body, the Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Yugoslavia (AVNOJ), first met at Bihać on 26 November 1942. At Jajce, from 21 to 29 November 1943, the AVNOJ's second session founded Democratic Federal Yugoslavia, a federation of six equal South Slav republics, named Tito prime minister and Marshal, and left the question of monarchy to a referendum.

The Tito–Šubašić Agreement of 17 June 1944 won the exiled king's recognition and a coalition government, and Belgrade was liberated with the Red Army in October 1944; by the end of April 1945 the whole country was free. In the first months after the war the Partisans executed alleged collaborators without trial until the autumn of 1945; the remaining 200,000 ethnic Germans lost their property and were interned before expulsion, and Italians in Dalmatia and Istria were killed in the foibe massacres or fled. The election of 11 November 1945, fairly voted but preceded by banned newspapers and threats, gave the People's Front an average of 85%; on 29 November the Constituent Assembly abolished the monarchy and proclaimed the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia.
sections.socioeconomy:
The war had killed over a million people, left 3.5 million homeless, wrecked 289,000 businesses, a third of industry and every mine. Work brigades of the young rebuilt under the slogan 'No rest while we're rebuilding!', aided by $553.8 million in foreign help. A Five-Year Plan of 1947 on the Soviet model built heavy industry and arms factories; between 1953 and 1960 industrial production grew 13.83% a year. After the break with Moscow the economy took its own path: in June 1950 workers' self-management gave elected councils control of enterprises and their profits, and the reforms of 1965 ended most state control of prices and wages and allowed small businesses of up to five employees. GDP grew 6.1% a year into the early 1980s and illiteracy fell from one in two in 1945 to 20% in 1961.

Prosperity rested partly on open borders. Three million foreign tourists visited Dalmatia in 1965 and 4.75 million in 1970, bringing $275 million, a tenth of federal revenue, by 1969; emigration was legalised in 1963, and by the early 1970s 1.1 million workers, a fifth of the labour force, worked abroad, two thirds in West Germany. The regions diverged: in 1965 Slovenia's income per head was 177.3% of the national figure and Kosovo's 38.6%. The oil shock of 1973–74 was met with borrowing that grew 20% a year; by the late 1980s unemployment passed 17%, real incomes had fallen 19.5%, inflation reached 2,700% in 1989 and the external debt $17 billion.
sections.military:
The armed forces were the Yugoslav People's Army (JNA), the Territorial Defence, Civil Defence and, in wartime, the police. All men served twelve months, with no alternative service and harsh treatment for objectors. Born of the Partisans, the army pursued self-sufficiency: by the mid-1950s virtually all its weapons were made at home, and its arms industry exported to non-aligned states and others such as Iraq and Ethiopia. After the Cominform expelled Yugoslavia in 1948 Soviet units massed on the Hungarian border and the Hungarian army grew from 2 to 15 divisions; the security service UDBA under Aleksandar Ranković crushed Cominformist plots, 55,600 party members were expelled and about 16,000 were sent to the camp on Goli Otok. American weapons arrived from 1951, but Yugoslavia refused to join NATO in 1953.

The Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968 convinced Tito that Yugoslavia would be next. His doctrine of 'all-people's defence' planned a fighting retreat into the interior and guerrilla war: in 1969 the forces were reorganised into 250,000 professional soldiers, 250,000 reservists and territorial defence forces of the six republics numbering some 900,000 men. By arming the population and giving each republic its own force, the reform later played a major part in the breakup, when the army factionalised along ethnic lines and by 1991–92 Serbs made up almost the whole of it while the seceding states raised their own.
sections.governance:
Yugoslavia was a one-party socialist federation ruled by the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, renamed the League of Communists of Yugoslavia at its Sixth Congress on 2 November 1952 and made a federation of six republican parties. Constitutions came in 1946 (amended 1953), 1963 and 1974; the Federal Assembly, entirely Communist, did little more than approve the Politburo's decisions, and Tito, elected President-for-life in 1974, was succeeded in 1980 by a collective presidency whose chair rotated among the republics. The six republics, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia and Slovenia, were constitutionally equal; Serbia alone contained two autonomous provinces, Kosovo and Vojvodina, which the 1974 constitution gave voting power equal to the republics', to the lasting anger of Serbian officials.

The regime was somewhat more humane than other Communist states but kept absolute power. Censorship was enforced by the republics, so an article banned in one could appear in another; a 1973 law restricted the media, and by 1975 Yugoslavia held 4,000 political prisoners, more than any European state but Albania and the Soviet Union. The Croatian Spring of 1971 was purged, and the dissident journal Praxis closed. Women gained the vote in 1945, Article 24 of the 1946 constitution declared their equality, and the Women's Antifascist Front campaigned against the full veil until it was banned in the 1950s.
sections.impact:
Yugoslavia's break with Stalin in 1948 was the first open rupture in the Eastern Bloc. Having liberated itself with little Soviet help, it refused subordination, answered the Cominform's charges of 'Trotskyism' and 'nationalist elements' and built a socialism of its own, 'Titoism', with workers' self-management as its hallmark. Refusing the Warsaw Pact and NATO alike, it became a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement with India, Egypt and Indonesia; Tito made 169 official visits to 92 nations and carried the Algerian FLN's demands to the United Nations.

Culturally the country belonged to the West more than to the Bloc: Western films and music were everywhere, foreign productions were shot on its locations, the 'black wave' of novels and films showed a corrupt and dehumanising society, and by the mid-1980s its rock scene was counted among the richest in Europe. Ivo Andrić won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1961; Yugoslavia entered the Eurovision Song Contest the same year and won it in 1989 with Riva's 'Rock Me'. Sarajevo hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics, Yugoslav basketball won world championships in 1970, 1978 and 1990 and Olympic gold in 1980, water polo took Olympic gold in 1968, 1984 and 1988, and Red Star Belgrade won the European Cup in 1991. The memory of the joint state, its stability, free travel, education and welfare, survives as Yugo-nostalgia, and the ties among its heirs are called the 'Yugosphere'.
sections.decline:
Tito died on 4 May 1980, aged 87, and the weakened federal system could not cope with what followed. Debt relief arranged by the 'Friends of Yugoslavia' in 1983 and 1984 did not stop unemployment and inflation soaring. Kosovo Albanians demanded a republic from the protests of 1981, and Serb opposition to the provinces' autonomy grew. In 1987 Slobodan Milošević came to power in Serbia and by populist means gained de facto control of Kosovo, Vojvodina and Montenegro, opposed by the leaders of Slovenia and Croatia. The League of Communists dissolved along federal lines in January 1990, and in that year's first multi-party elections ethnic separatist parties won everywhere but Serbia and Montenegro.

Between June 1991 and April 1992 four republics declared independence: Croatia and Slovenia on 25 June 1991, Macedonia on 25 September 1991 and Bosnia and Herzegovina on 3 March 1992. Germany recognised Croatia and Slovenia, but the status of Serbs outside Serbia and Croats outside Croatia was unresolved, and the Yugoslav Wars of 1991–2001 followed, most severely in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo. On 27 April 1992 the Federal Council adopted the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for Serbia and Montenegro, formally ending the breakup; in September 1992 the United Nations refused to treat it as the continuation of the SFRY; the Badinter Commission found that Yugoslavia had dissolved rather than suffered secessions.

summary: The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Tito's federation of six South Slav republics proclaimed in 1945, broke with Stalin in 1948 and built a socialism of workers' self-management, open borders and non-alignment that made it the most prosperous and liberal of the Communist states, until debt, nationalism and the loss of its leader in 1980 dissolved it in the Yugoslav Wars by 1992.
references: Marie-Janine Calic, A History of Yugoslavia (Purdue University Press, 2019)
John R. Lampe, Yugoslavia as History: Twice There Was a Country (Cambridge University Press, 1996)

pointDescs.1945: The Partisans liberate the whole country by the end of April; the People's Front wins the election of 11 November and the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia is proclaimed on 29 November.
pointDescs.1946: The first constitution comes into force and the six federated states become people's republics; reconstruction begins with work brigades and UN aid, and two American aircraft are shot down in August.
pointDescs.1948: The Cominform expels Yugoslavia on 28 June; the economy, oriented to the Eastern Bloc, falters, Soviet troops mass on the Hungarian border and the UDBA hunts Cominformists.
pointDescs.1950: Workers' self-management is introduced in June under the Basic Law drafted by Kardelj, Djilas, Pijade, Kidrič and Bakarić; Western aid averts famine.
pointDescs.1953: Yugoslavia refuses to join NATO while taking American arms; industrial production begins to grow 13.83% a year through 1960.
pointDescs.1961: Ivo Andrić wins the Nobel Prize, Yugoslavia enters the Eurovision Song Contest, and the country is a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement; foreign observers call the economy 'booming'.
pointDescs.1965: Market reforms end most state control of prices and wages; three million foreign tourists visit Dalmatia; Bosnian Muslims become a sixth nationality; a development fund is created for the poorer republics.
pointDescs.1968: Student protests in June force a change of policy; after the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia Tito builds 'all-people's defence', giving each republic its own territorial army.
pointDescs.1971: The Croatian Spring is purged and the republics gain control of their economic plans; 775,000 Yugoslavs work abroad.
pointDescs.1974: The third constitution grants the republics and the provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina wide autonomy and makes Tito President-for-life; the borrowed prosperity of the 1970s is at its height.
pointDescs.1980: Tito dies on 4 May; a collective presidency takes over a state with growing foreign debt.
pointDescs.1984: Sarajevo hosts the Winter Olympics and the 'Friends of Yugoslavia' arrange debt relief, but unemployment and inflation keep rising.
pointDescs.1987: Slobodan Milošević comes to power in Serbia and gains de facto control of Kosovo, Vojvodina and Montenegro, opposed by Slovenia and Croatia.
pointDescs.1989: Inflation reaches 2,700%, external debt $17 billion; Yugoslavia wins Eurovision with 'Rock Me' as communism falls across Eastern Europe.
pointDescs.1990: The League of Communists dissolves in January; separatist parties win the first multi-party elections everywhere but Serbia and Montenegro.
pointDescs.1991: Croatia and Slovenia declare independence on 25 June and Macedonia on 25 September; the Yugoslav Wars begin.
pointDescs.1992: Bosnia and Herzegovina declares independence on 3 March; on 27 April Serbia and Montenegro adopt the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, formally ending the SFRY.

notes: The article's Sources section is empty; its text names only Marie-Janine Calic (no title) and External links (a CIA report of 1970, Daniel Jakopovich's 'Yugoslavia's Self-Management'), so [] is given.

The article says the Free Territory of Trieste was dissolved 'in 1954 ... by the Treaty of Osimo'; the profile leaves Trieste out of the sections (the editor may wish to check that date and name before any use).
The Non-Aligned Movement's founding is undated in the article; the 1961 point names it without a date of foundation.
The article gives the 1989 unemployment rate as 15% in its indicators and 'over 17%' in the late 1980s in its text; the text's figure is used.

The 1965 point calls Bosnian Muslims a 'sixth nationality' as the article's Ethnic issues section does; its Demographics section lists them among the 'nations' from 1971. Cut from the governance section for length, with the Macedonian nation (1945), Ranković's fall (1966) and the UDBA's assassinations of exiles.

Yugoslav support for the Greek Communists, the Trieste crisis, the Balkan Federation talks and the foibe massacres are from the article; the 'Jews' and 'Kosovo 1945 uprising' matters are omitted for length.
The 1992 Badinter finding (dissolution, not secession) and the UN's refusal of continuation in September 1992 are given in the decline section.
